beats.label: Light arrives
beats.narration: Light arrives at a solar panel in tiny packets of energy called photons. The panel is made up of smaller units called solar cells.

beats.label: Electrons move
beats.narration: Electrons can break free when a solar cell absorbs enough light energy. The cell is built to push those freed charges in a preferred direction.

beats.label: Direct current
beats.narration: Direct current flows when a circuit gives the charges a path. Inside that circuit, electricity moves in one direction, like traffic on a one way street.

beats.label: Alternating current
beats.narration: Alternating current is what most household appliances use. An inverter changes the panel's direct current into alternating current so it can power those devices.

beats.label: Sun and shade
beats.narration: Sun and shade affect how much energy reaches each cell. A rooftop system usually makes more electricity in direct sunlight than under heavy cloud or shade.

beats.label: Follow the energy
beats.narration: Follow the energy from sunlight to moving charges, through an inverter, and into your home. That is the basic path from a sunny roof to a working appliance.

beats.label: Weather
beats.narration: Weather describes the conditions around you now or soon. If you are deciding whether to take an umbrella this afternoon, you want a weather forecast.

beats.label: Climate
beats.narration: Climate describes patterns over many years. If you are deciding which crops normally grow in a region, the long term pattern is what you need.

beats.label: A cold afternoon
beats.narration: A cold afternoon can happen during a warm year. One observation tells you something about that time and place, but it cannot tell you whether a long term trend has changed.

beats.label: Years of records
beats.narration: Years of records let you compare averages and look at how common extreme events are. Climate is about how the whole pattern behaves, including its variation.

beats.label: Plan today
beats.narration: Plan today with the weather forecast. Check the predicted rain and temperature for the hours when you will actually be outdoors.

beats.label: Plan ahead
beats.narration: Plan ahead with climate records. The same thermometer can help answer both questions, but only when you use measurements across the time period that matters.

beats.label: One free hour
beats.narration: One free hour gives you several choices. You could practise guitar, call a friend, or watch a show. You can only spend that same hour once.

beats.label: Best alternative
beats.narration: Best alternative means the option you would choose if your first choice disappeared. Suppose you practise guitar, and calling a friend would have been your next choice.

beats.label: Money paid
beats.narration: Money paid is what leaves your wallet. Practising guitar at home may cost nothing today, so the immediate price can be zero.

beats.label: Value forgone
beats.narration: Value forgone is what you give up by making the choice. In this example, it is the value of the time you would have spent talking to your friend.

beats.label: Name the alternative
beats.narration: Name the alternative you would realistically take. You do not add up every option you skipped, because you could not have done all of them.

beats.label: Compare the value
beats.narration: Compare the value of your choice with that next best alternative. Thinking this way helps you notice the trade off, even when there is no price tag.
